title_tag: 特朗普的「致命豪赌」：从权力无限到被选民彻底否定 —— 美国《华尔街日报》外刊讲解第1220天
h1: 特朗普的「致命豪赌」：从权力无限到被选民彻底否定，只用了几个月
category: 美国《华尔街日报》外刊讲解 第1220天

paragraphs.en_html: In mid-February, one of President Trump’s economic advisers arrived at the Oval Office with charts showing how the administration’s policies might be making America great again. Household income was up, particularly among low-income Americans. Retirement accounts were soaring. And the nation’s economic growth was even better than projected. “This is great stuff,” said Trump. He had completed his first year back in office, and his power seemed limitless.

Within days, Trump made a decision that would change everything. After campaigning on ending foreign wars, Trump wagered on one of his own, triggering an open-ended conflict that has seen the deaths of more than 20 U.S. servicemembers, cost U.S. taxpayers more than $47 billion, and pushed up the cost of everything from freight to fertilizer. On Tuesday, Republicans suffered losses that amounted to one of the most decisive repudiations of a president in modern history. It was likely a direct result of Trump’s decision to go to war in Iran, sending gas prices up 40%, leaving many of his most loyal supporters disillusioned and effectively drawing a curtain on the Trump age.

Conservative commentator Matt Walsh described the war as “the greatest political blunder in the last two decades,” and a betrayal of Trump’s America First movement. “We’re going to have to find a new leader because Trump abandoned it,” he said in an interview. While Trump publicly defended the war, privately he asked people around him whether he should change course, including junior staffers who gathered for a photo. The war wasn’t the only issue contributing to Tuesday’s crushing defeat for Republicans. Trump also lost his advantage on immigration. After first lady Melania Trump complained about people she knew getting deported, the president would tell aides that the architect of his aggressive immigration campaign, Stephen Miller, had gone too far.

When Trump’s aides told him in the spring and summer that polls showed voters concerned about his handling of affordability, he said the polling was fake, the senior administration official said. Trump also pushed out of Senate races Republican candidates who would have faced better odds, including in Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina and Texas. He instead anointed candidates he believed would be loyal to him. Democrats won in all four of these states. “It really didn’t have to be this way,” said Rep. Ralph Norman, the Republican who lost the South Carolina Republican nomination to Sen. Darline Graham after Trump swooped in. “Pride goeth before the fall. It’s going to be a wake-up call for the Republican Party.”

By August, polls showed Republicans had lost their edge with voters on the economy. Trump aides grew deeply concerned in August when internal polling showed voters overwhelmingly blamed Trump for inflation over Democrats. In September, gasoline prices in the U.S. shot up 16 cents in a single week. Not long after, diesel prices hit a record high. On one Republican call, a pollster said, “People will mark the last week of September as the week the bottom fell out.”

When Trump wanted to veto a popular bipartisan housing bill, senior White House official James Braid sent a note to other staffers asking them to help persuade the president to sign it. Trump shut down the lawmakers and advisers favoring the bill, scuttling a news conference so late that some lawmakers arrived anyway. Nobody cares about this, he told one adviser. Aides eventually persuaded him to let the housing bill become law without his signature.

Allegations of corruption involving the administration and the Trump family became a top concern for voters. Yet Trump continued to focus on pet projects, including a new White House ballroom and a proposed 250-foot triumphal arch. He interrupted Oval Office meetings to show off his latest plans, at one point leading a guest outside to see how he attached gold letters reading “The Rose Garden.” Aides said it was a waste of time to tell him to stop talking about the ballroom because he held several long meetings a week on the topic and enjoyed giving tours.

On Monday, the day before the midterm election, Trump gave a nearly hourlong speech at the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool that aides had billed as a final argument to voters. Trump mostly talked about his renovations of the capital, including cleaning up graffiti, resodding the mall and replacing rusty pipes. One of the project’s biggest foes, he said, had been algae. There wasn’t enough time, he said, to discuss his plans for the nation. “The biggest issue is that I wasn’t on the ballot,” he told The Wall Street Journal. Yet, Trump had said repeatedly that voters should imagine that he was on the ballot.

By October, some Republicans felt that a spending blitz by Republican super PACs, including Trump’s MAGA Inc., would stabilize the map. The money couldn’t compete with gas prices and other pocketbook troubles. “It was about the economy,” said Chris Winkelman, president of the Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC run by Johnson allies. “It was always about the economy.”
